summary.text: A 27-year-old woman arrived at the emergency room about 4 h after ingesting about 20 mL of 24% paraquat with suicidal intent, with nausea, vomiting, sore throat and epigastric pain. She reported no underlying medical problems and worked on a farm with access to herbicides. Vital signs were recorded, and her oral mucosa was erythematous and edematous.
Initial laboratory results, ECG and chest X-ray were normal. The urine dithionite test was strongly positive, confirming paraquat, and the blood paraquat level at 6 h after ingestion was 1.98 ug/mL.

She received activated charcoal, sorbitol via nasogastric tube, intravenous fluid and analgesics, was admitted to the ICU and was given a repeated charcoal and sorbitol dose. Over the next 24 h her epigastric pain increased with severe dysphagia and shortness of breath, and a chest radiograph showed infiltration; on ICU day 2 urea, creatinine and liver enzymes were elevated and arterial blood gas values were recorded.

On Day 3 the chest radiograph showed bilateral infiltrates, pneumomediastinum and pneumopericardium; she became hypoxemic and was intubated and ventilated, her renal function deteriorated and hemodialysis was started. Progressive multiple-organ failure followed and she died on Day 4 after admission.

summary.text: A 35-year-old woman was admitted to the emergency room on May 31, 2023 at around 7 pm, approximately 3.5 h after ingesting paraquat dichloride with suicidal intent, and she had also poisoned her two sons. She was stable with intact consciousness and an open airway; initial examination and laboratory tests, including blood count and renal and liver function, were within normal limits.

She received intravenous pantoprazole, ondansetron and fluids and was moved to the MICU, where she had dry mouth, oral redness, tongue ulcers and odynophagia and received dexamethasone, N-acetylcysteine, vitamin C, topical Delta gel and chlorhexidine mouthwash. Psychiatric consultation found persistent low mood, disturbed sleep and anger but no psychotic symptoms. On the third day polyuria, creatinine 1.07 mg/dL and potassium 3.04 mmol/L were treated with vasopressin and potassium chloride.

On the fourth day urine output was maintained on a vasopressor that was subsequently stopped. Acute kidney injury resolved, but bradycardia with a heart rate of 28 bpm and hypokalemia developed, and N-acetylcysteine and vasopressin therapy were continued. Her condition stabilized on the fifth day and she moved to the high-dependency unit with oral potassium supplementation.

On June 7 psychiatric evaluation diagnosed a severe depressive episode with Hamilton Depression Rating Scale 23 and Suicidal Intent scale 17. Gastroenterology and ENT consultations for throat pain led to sucralfate syrup and antiseptic mouthwash, and after 19 days of treatment and counseling she was discharged on June 19, 2023.

summary.text: A 7-year-old boy was given paraquat mixed with milk by his mother and was admitted to CMCTH on May 31, 2023 at around 7 pm; he vomited twice with greenish contents, and the exact time since ingestion was unclear. At a nearby hospital he received ceftriaxone and ranitidine before referral, and on arrival he was ill-looking and drowsy with GCS 14/15, respiratory rate 24, oxygen saturation 98% on room air and heart rate 105.

He received intravenous ondansetron in the ER, was moved to the PICU for observation, had one more vomiting episode treated with ondansetron and remained hemodynamically stable before transfer to the ward. Urea 143 mg/dL and creatinine 2 mg/dL were elevated with increased cortical echogenicity in both kidneys on ultrasound, and after 2 days urea was 141 mg/dL and creatinine 2.14 mg/dL.

A cough with wheezing resolved after nebulization with salbutamol and budesonide. By the day of discharge urea was 90 mg/dL and creatinine 1.54 mg/dL, both returned to normal; he was stable with normal urine output and was discharged after 8 days with improved renal and pulmonary function, a prescription for Foracort via mask and spacer and follow-up instructions.

summary.text: A 1-year-old boy with global developmental delay, dystonia and seizure disorder was brought to CMCTH on May 31, 2023 at 7 pm after his mother mixed paraquat with milk; he cried excessively, had worsening dystonic postures with backward arching and three episodes of vomiting, and had no history of cyanosis, abnormal body movements or external bleeding. He was first managed at a nearby hospital with oxygen, ceftriaxone, ranitidine and hydrocortisone.

On arrival in the ER he was in critical condition with an unstable airway and audible stridor, respiratory rate 71, heart rate 195, temperature 101.9 F and SpO2 91% on a facemask, with hypertonia and dystonia, GCS 14/15, muscle power 3/5, crusted lips and erythematous oral mucosa. He received dexamethasone, adrenaline nebulization, paracetamol and CPAP, which raised SpO2 to 95%; IV cannulation failed and no blood samples were collected.

In the PICU he continued CPAP, dexamethasone and adrenaline, then had a generalized tonic-clonic seizure aborted with midazolam, worsening sensorium with central cyanosis and desaturation, and was resuscitated with bag and mask ventilation and endotracheal intubation. At around 6 h of PICU admission he developed bradycardia below 60 and, despite resuscitation, was declared dead 7 h after admission.

article_limitations: The article has no figures, tables or supplements.
The paragraph about the seizure, intubation, bradycardia and death does not name the younger son; it is attributed from the preceding paragraph and the abstract.

The discussion sentence that all patients ingested more than 20 mL of 24% PQ literally conflicts with the case-text amounts for the mother (20 mL) and younger son (approximately 5 mL) and with the elder son spitting the poison out; both sides of each conflict are review-only and only the amount is quarantined.
